quorum.kill_rule: six claims and the standing instruction. THE FIXTURE DID NOT REPRODUCE THE SHAPE: squash_claiming ended at the trailer block, so git parsed it and six of the nine cases would have passed over an arm rewritten to use git's own trailer parser — the one regression the suite exists to prevent. Found by following a single false sentence about how GitHub writes a squash message.
refuted_claims: That a squash message ends with whatever bullets GitHub assembled. GitHub appends its own last paragraph — a --------- separator and a Co-authored-by block — and that is what pushes the Pmat-Ticket lines out of git's view.
That the fixture reproduces the shape that makes git blind. squash_claiming ended at the trailer block, git parsed it, and every case would have passed over an arm using git's parser.
That the floor comment's arithmetic matches the log: it said 28 agree against a log measuring 29 over 30 rows, because #496 agrees after alias resolution.
That section 3 of the log shows a floor at main's tip. It contrasts the shipped floor with a floor this repository does not carry.
That gate A enforces what CLAUDE.md promised — that the merge commit CLAIMS the ticket. A commit claiming nothing passes, deliberately, so the promise was what was wrong.
That every command in the arm can fail safely. The claims pipeline had no exit guard, so a failure would have killed the gate with no GATE A line — a death rather than a verdict.
That the arm closes the misattribution. A merge commit claiming two tickets under a PR filed as one passes, and a PR and its commits agreeing on a lie pass: the arm measures agreement, not truth.

Chef Expeditor (the merge label, written by a bot, is the only source of the version bump)
Kubernetes Prow (release-note blocks are adjudicated from the PR body by a bot at merge time)
crux.verdict: accept(each surveyed system binds a change to its work item through a field a TOOL writes and a TOOL reads, and each puts the check where the binding can still be changed — Gerrit on the server at push, Prow at merge. forjar reads the binding from a BRANCH NAME, free text nobody validated, in three gates; PMAT-535 checks it at push and this checks it after merge, which is the last place the two sources are both visible. Where forjar is WORSE than Gerrit: this refuses the RELEASE rather than the merge, so a misattributed PR lands and is caught by make dogfood-release afterwards. Where it is better than the kernel's tooling: the reader is told what the id DECIDES — a receipt path, a quorum filename and a release window — rather than only that it disagreed.)
